stories.title: India's factories and services hire at the fastest pace in nearly 20 years, PMI shows — even as the stock market slides
key_points: HSBC flash India Composite PMI rose to 61.4 in July, a 3-month high
Services PMI hit a 4-month high of 61.1; manufacturing rose to 58.5
Job creation grew at its fastest pace since April 2006
Comes even as Sensex and Nifty fall for a fifth straight day
stories.background: The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) is a monthly survey of company managers that gauges whether business activity is expanding or shrinking — a reading above 50 means growth. India's PMI has stayed above 50 for roughly three straight years, one of the strongest expansion streaks of any major economy, even as global growth has cooled.
stories.what_happened: S&P Global/HSBC's flash India Composite PMI climbed to 61.4 in July from June's final 60.9, driven by strong services demand (PMI 61.1) and a pickup in manufacturing (58.5, the highest since April). Companies reported hiring at the fastest pace since April 2006 as order books grew.
stories.why_it_matters: The reading shows India's real economy staying resilient even as its stock market has fallen for five straight sessions on oil-price and foreign-investor worries tied to the Iran war. It suggests the sell-off is being driven more by global jitters than by weakness in the underlying Indian economy.
stories.ripple_effects: Strong hiring and output data support the case for the Reserve Bank of India to hold interest rates rather than cut them, and give the government a positive data point even as inflation risks build from costlier oil. Sustained job growth also feeds consumer spending, the biggest driver of India's GDP.
stories.why_now: This is the first full read on how Indian businesses are coping with both the global oil-price shock from the Iran war and the new US 'forced-labour' tariff — and it shows they're coping well so far.
stories.watch_next: Watch the final PMI reading due in early August, and whether hiring momentum holds if oil stays above $100 a barrel for an extended period.

key_terms.definition: A monthly survey-based score where above 50 means business activity is growing and below 50 means it's shrinking — one of the fastest available reads on how an economy is doing.

stories.the_lesson: A country's stock market and its real economy can move in opposite directions at the same time — a falling Sensex reflects investor sentiment and global risk appetite, not necessarily what's happening on factory floors and in offices.
stories.market_link: Strong PMI data is typically read as good news for Indian equities and the rupee over time, though it's being overshadowed this week by oil-driven FII (foreign institutional investor) selling.

stories.title: Sensex and Nifty fall for a fifth straight day as oil tops $100 on the Iran war
key_points: Sensex fell 331 points, Nifty fell 102 points to close at 23,767
Fifth straight losing session for both indices
Auto, metal and energy stocks led the fall; IT and media held up
Driven by crude oil spiking past $100/barrel on the Iran war and Houthi attacks
stories.background: Yesterday we reported the Sensex and Nifty fell for a fourth straight day as Gulf tensions pushed oil higher. That selloff has now stretched to a fifth day as the region's violence escalates further — continued US strikes on Iran and fresh Houthi missile attacks on Saudi tankers — pushing crude oil, a major cost for import-dependent India, even higher.
stories.what_happened: The Sensex closed at 76,059.77, down 331.62 points (0.43%); the Nifty 50 closed at 23,767.45, down 102.15 points (0.43%) — the fifth consecutive losing session for both indices. Auto, metal and energy stocks dragged the market down, while IT and media stocks gained.
stories.why_it_matters: A five-day losing streak is unusual and signals investors see the Middle East conflict as a sustained threat to India's economy, not a one-day scare. Higher oil prices raise costs across the economy for a country that imports roughly 85% of its crude.
stories.ripple_effects: Expensive oil pushes up India's import bill and can widen the current-account deficit, which tends to weaken the rupee. It also raises transport and input costs for businesses, which can filter into consumer inflation and eventually pressure the RBI on interest-rate decisions. Energy and auto stocks, heavy fuel users, feel it first.
stories.why_now: The Houthis opened a 'second front' this week by firing on two more Saudi oil tankers, adding fresh supply-risk premium onto crude that was already elevated from the US-Iran conflict — that's what's pushing oil, and hurting Indian equities, today.
stories.watch_next: Watch Brent crude's level — a sustained move above $100/barrel is what would force the RBI and government to worry seriously about inflation and the rupee.

key_terms.definition: The gap between what a country pays for imports (like oil) and what it earns from exports — a bigger gap usually weakens its currency.

stories.the_lesson: When a country depends heavily on imported oil, its stock market becomes a real-time barometer of geopolitical risk half a world away — a missile in the Red Sea can move a portfolio in Mumbai the same day.
stories.market_link: Directly a markets story — Sensex/Nifty, auto/metal/energy stocks, crude oil, and by extension the rupee.

thread.previously: We reported a fourth straight day of losses as Gulf tensions pushed oil prices higher.
thread.changed: The losing streak has extended to a fifth day, with oil now topping $100/barrel and auto, metal and energy stocks leading the decline.

stories.title: Sonam Wangchuk ends his 26-day hunger strike after two ministers step in — but the protests don't stop
key_points: Wangchuk ends fast after 26 days, following talks with two federal ministers
PM Modi pledges a tougher anti-paper-leak law in a video address
Protesters vow to continue until the Education Minister resigns
His fast had become the rallying symbol of India's 'Cockroach' protest movement
stories.background: Sonam Wangchuk is a Ladakh-based education reformer and climate activist. He began a hunger strike over exam paper leaks, and yesterday we reported his health crisis was deepening, with a Delhi court ordering him moved to a private hospital. His strike became the anchor of the 'Cockroach' protest movement — a youth-led wave of demonstrations that began more than a month ago demanding education reforms after leaks in major competitive entrance exams.
stories.what_happened: Wangchuk ended his 26-day hunger strike on Friday, in the presence of two federal ministers, after what he called 'a long negotiation... in view of possible violence in the country.' His announcement followed a video message from PM Modi promising a tougher law against paper leaks and fast-track courts. Protest organizers said demonstrations will continue until Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns.
stories.why_it_matters: One of India's largest protest movements in recent years just lost its most visible symbol — but not its demands. Whether the government's promised legal changes satisfy protesters, or the leaderless 'Cockroach' movement keeps growing without him, will shape how India's paper-leak crisis plays out.
stories.ripple_effects: The government gets relief from the immediate, life-threatening pressure of the hunger strike, but not necessarily political cover — daily demonstrations may continue regardless. Wangchuk remains a national figure whose health scare drew wide coverage; how he re-engages next could reshape the movement's direction.
stories.why_now: His health had deteriorated to the point of hospitalization, as we reported yesterday — with two ministers and dozens of MPs appealing directly and warning of 'possible violence', ending the fast now averts both a health crisis and a public-order risk.
stories.watch_next: Watch whether the promised tougher anti-paper-leak law appears in Parliament, and whether Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan faces continued pressure to resign.

key_terms.definition: A nickname for India's youth-led protest wave demanding education reform after major entrance-exam paper leaks — the name stuck after officials dismissively compared protesters to pests.

stories.the_lesson: A hunger strike works as protest leverage because it puts a clock on the government's response — but ending the strike doesn't end the underlying demand. Movements built around one person's health crisis have to find a way to keep pressure on once that person steps back.

thread.previously: We reported his hunger-strike health crisis deepening, with a Delhi court ordering him moved to a private hospital.
thread.changed: He has now ended the 26-day fast after direct intervention from two federal ministers and a PM Modi pledge on a tougher anti-paper-leak law, though protesters vow to continue until the education minister resigns.

stories.title: Commonwealth Games debutant Putul Sonowal, 43, stuns the reigning world bowls champion to open India's campaign
key_points: Sonowal beat seven-time world medalist Ryan Bester of Canada in a tie-break
It was Sonowal's first-ever Commonwealth Games match, at age 43
Pinki Singh and Rupa Rani Tirkey also won their bowls match against Malta
Marks one of the biggest upsets of the Games' opening day
stories.background: Lawn bowls is a precision sport where players roll weighted balls to land closest to a target ball — it isn't widely followed in India, but the country has quietly built a competitive team, including winning historic medals at the 2022 Commonwealth Games. Ryan Bester is one of the sport's most decorated players, with seven World Outdoor Championship medals.
stories.what_happened: On the opening day of bowls at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, India's Putul Sonowal — the reigning Asian champion making his Games debut at 43 — beat Canada's Ryan Bester in a tie-break after the two split the first two sets. In a separate match, India's Pinki Singh and Rupa Rani Tirkey beat Malta.
stories.why_it_matters: Beating a seven-time world medalist on debut is a signature underdog result that puts India's bowls team on the map early in the Games, and gives the country's broader medal push a psychological boost heading into higher-profile events like boxing and para-powerlifting.
stories.ripple_effects: A strong start in bowls adds to India's overall medal tally push and could draw more domestic attention — and future funding — to a sport that otherwise gets little coverage in India.
stories.why_now: This happened on the opening day of Commonwealth Games competition and is part of India's broader push for medals across multiple sports this week.
stories.watch_next: Watch how far Sonowal advances in the individual singles bracket over the coming days.
stories.the_lesson: In global multi-sport events, unheralded athletes in niche disciplines can produce some of the biggest upsets — medal tallies aren't only won in the sports that get the most attention.

stories.title: Government removes its Higher Education Secretary as accountability pressure mounts over the NEET paper leak
key_points: Vineet Joshi is out as Higher Education Secretary, transferred to the Panchayati Raj ministry
IAS officer Naresh Pal Gangwar, previously at the fisheries ministry, takes over
Move comes amid nationwide protests and demands for Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation
Follows PM Modi's announcement of fast-track courts for paper-leak cases
stories.background: India's medical entrance exam, NEET-UG, was hit by a leak scandal that triggered nationwide student protests, a hunger strike by activist Sonam Wangchuk, and days of disruption in Parliament as the opposition demanded Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resign. The government has been under growing pressure to show it is taking the leak seriously rather than just making promises.
stories.what_happened: The government replaced Vineet Joshi as Secretary of the Department of Higher Education with Naresh Pal Gangwar, a 1994-batch IAS officer who was serving as Secretary of the Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying. Joshi has been shifted to the Department of Panchayati Raj. The change comes directly amid the ongoing NEET-UG paper-leak protests.
stories.why_it_matters: Removing the top bureaucrat overseeing higher education is a visible sign the government is treating this as more than a PR problem — it's a personnel accountability move, not just a policy announcement. Coming right after Modi's fast-track courts pledge, it suggests a coordinated response before the protest movement grows further.
stories.ripple_effects: This could ease some pressure on Education Minister Pradhan by giving the opposition a bureaucratic scalp instead of a ministerial one, but protest groups may see it as insufficient and keep pushing for Pradhan's resignation. It also puts Gangwar under an immediate spotlight to show visible reform in how exams are secured.
stories.why_now: This is surfacing today because the transfer order was issued this week, directly amid the nationwide paper-leak strike and protest movement covered in today's feed.
stories.watch_next: Watch for whether Gangwar announces concrete anti-leak measures for the next exam cycle, and whether protest leaders consider this enough to stand down.

key_terms.definition: A member of the Indian Administrative Service — the senior civil servants who run government ministries and departments day-to-day, regardless of which party is in power.

stories.the_lesson: When a government faces sustained public pressure over a failure, removing the official most directly responsible is often the fastest way to show accountability — even before the underlying policy problem itself is fixed.

thread.previously: Modi announced the government would set up fast-track courts to deliver swift punishment in paper-leak cases, as pressure built from Wangchuk's hunger strike and the 'Cockroach' movement.
thread.changed: The government has now also removed the top bureaucrat overseeing higher education, Vineet Joshi, replacing him with Naresh Pal Gangwar — a more direct personnel accountability move alongside the earlier court pledge.

stories.title: Supreme Court bars anyone from posting or monetizing courtroom video clips without official permission
key_points: Interim order bans posting, editing, or monetizing live-streamed court footage on social media
Prior permission is now needed from the Supreme Court's Secretary General or the relevant High Court's Registrar General
Order came on a plea by journalist Harshita Grover over misuse of court livestreams
News reporting of court proceedings is explicitly NOT affected
stories.background: India began live-streaming select Supreme Court and High Court hearings in recent years to boost transparency. But that footage has increasingly been clipped, edited out of context, and reposted on YouTube and social media — sometimes to sensationalize exchanges between judges and lawyers, or to monetize clips through ad revenue. A journalist, Harshita Grover, filed a public interest litigation asking the Court to set clear rules for how livestreamed proceedings can be used.
stories.what_happened: A three-judge bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, along with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana, passed an interim order stating there shall be no extraction, editing, dissemination, posting, reposting, uploading, or monetization of audio-video recordings of court proceedings on social media or any digital platform without prior permission from the Secretary General of the Supreme Court or the Registrar General of the relevant High Court. The bench also asked High Courts to report back on what rules they already have for regulating livestreamed hearings. The Court clarified this does not restrict ordinary news reporting.
stories.why_it_matters: This directly affects the fast-growing ecosystem of legal-commentary YouTube channels and social media pages that build audiences — and ad revenue — by clipping courtroom moments, some of which have previously drawn criticism for misrepresenting exchanges or embarrassing judges and litigants. It's also a broader test of how India balances open-court transparency against the risk of court proceedings being turned into out-of-context viral content.
stories.ripple_effects: Legal-content creators and news channels that rely on courtroom video clips will need to seek formal clearance or risk takedowns; it may also push High Courts to formalize their own livestream-usage rules following the Supreme Court's request for reports.
stories.why_now: The order was prompted by a specific PIL flagging the growing volume of edited, monetized courtroom clips circulating online, at a time when court livestreaming has become far more common across Indian courts.
stories.watch_next: Whether the High Courts' reports on their existing livestream rules lead the Supreme Court to issue a more permanent, detailed framework beyond this interim order.

key_terms.definition: A petition filed in an Indian court not for personal relief but to protect a broader public interest — here, orderly and non-exploitative use of court livestreams.
A temporary court direction issued while a case is still being heard, meant to hold the situation steady until a final ruling.

stories.the_lesson: Transparency measures like court livestreaming can create new problems of their own — once footage is public, controlling how it's edited and monetized becomes a separate fight from the original goal of open justice.

stories.title: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain guarantees India a medal at the Commonwealth Games — without throwing a punch
key_points: Lovlina advances straight to the women's 75kg semifinal on a bye
Only five boxers entered that weight category, so the bye is automatic
Commonwealth Games boxing awards bronze to both losing semifinalists
She'll fight Tuvalu's Tarona Taafaki on July 31 for a place in the gold-medal match
stories.background: Lovlina Borgohain is one of India's best-known Olympic boxers, having won bronze at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics. At the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, she is India's flag-bearer and one of its top medal hopes. Commonwealth Games boxing uses a knockout format where both semifinal losers receive bronze — a quirk that means simply reaching the final four locks in a medal.
stories.what_happened: Because only five athletes entered the women's 75kg category, the draw left one boxer with no quarterfinal opponent. Lovlina Borgohain, Australia's Emma-Sue Greentree, and Tuvalu's Tarona Taafaki all advanced directly to the semifinals via byes. That guarantees Lovlina at least a bronze medal — India's first confirmed medal of the Games — before she has thrown a single punch. She now faces Taafaki in the semifinal on July 31, with a place in the gold-medal bout on the line.
stories.why_it_matters: For a team as large as India's at a multi-sport Games, an early, guaranteed medal is a psychological boost for the wider contingent and a talking point back home, even though the manner of it (a bye) means Lovlina hasn't actually beaten anyone yet.
stories.ripple_effects: It raises expectations on Lovlina to convert the guaranteed bronze into silver or gold, and puts more scrutiny on India's other boxers and combat-sport athletes to deliver similar returns as the Games progress.
stories.why_now: The Commonwealth Games opened this week in Glasgow, and boxing draws were finalized as competition got underway, exposing the small five-boxer field in the 75kg category.
stories.watch_next: Lovlina's semifinal against Tarona Taafaki on July 31, which decides whether India's guaranteed bronze becomes a shot at gold.

key_terms.definition: In a knockout tournament, a bye means a competitor advances to the next round automatically without having to play a match, usually because there's an odd number of entrants.

stories.the_lesson: In knockout sports formats, a guaranteed medal isn't always the same as a proven win — the size and structure of a draw can hand an athlete a result before they've competed, which is worth knowing before reading too much into a 'medal secured' headline.

stories.title: Hindustan Zinc's profit more than doubles on record zinc and silver prices
key_points: Q1 FY27 net profit up 144.81% year-on-year to ₹5,469 crore
Revenue rose about 72% to ₹13,033 crore on higher metal prices
Highest-ever first-quarter mined metal output: 268,000 tonnes, 5th year running
Result beats Street expectations of a strong but smaller jump
stories.background: Hindustan Zinc is the world's second-largest integrated zinc-lead-silver producer, mining and smelting in Rajasthan. It was privatised in stages from 2002, with Vedanta Ltd now the majority owner and the Indian government still holding a roughly 29.5% stake, so results also matter for public dividend income.
stories.what_happened: For the April-June 2026 quarter (Q1 of FY27, India's financial year running April-March), Hindustan Zinc reported consolidated net profit of ₹5,469 crore, up 144.81% from ₹2,234 crore a year earlier, on revenue up roughly 72% to about ₹13,033 crore. CEO Arun Misra said the company delivered its highest-ever first-quarter mined metal production of 268 KT (thousand tonnes) for the fifth straight year, crediting cost discipline and strong global zinc and silver prices even as production volumes typically dip in this quarter for seasonal reasons.
stories.why_it_matters: The scale of the jump — profit more than doubling — signals how much a sharp rise in global zinc and silver prices this year has flowed straight through to the bottom line of India's dominant zinc producer, reinforcing its position as one of the world's lowest-cost producers even as many other Indian companies report soft or mixed June-quarter results.
stories.ripple_effects: Stronger cash flow strengthens parent company Vedanta's finances and its capacity to pay dividends, some of which flow to the Indian government as a shareholder; the results are also likely to lift sentiment across India's broader metals and mining sector (peers like Vedanta, Hindalco and Tata Steel report around the same period), and could influence how investors price commodity-linked stocks amid a choppy broader market.
stories.why_now: The result was released today as part of India's June-quarter (Q1 FY27) earnings season, alongside roughly 80 other companies including NTPC, SBI Life and Bank of Baroda reporting on July 24.
stories.watch_next: Management's commentary on the 4pm earnings call about FY27 volume guidance and whether elevated zinc and silver prices are expected to hold through the rest of the year.

key_terms.definition: The company's total profit including its subsidiaries, after all costs and taxes.
The tonnage of raw metal-bearing ore extracted and processed, a measure of operational output separate from prices.
The first quarter (April-June 2026) of India's 2026-27 financial year, which runs April to March.

stories.the_lesson: For commodity producers, a blowout profit number often reflects rising global prices as much as — or more than — the company's own operational performance, so it's worth checking how much of the gain is price-driven versus volume- or efficiency-driven before assuming it will repeat.
stories.market_link: Direct — HINDZINC shares and read-through to metals/mining peers (Vedanta, Hindalco, Tata Steel) and the Nifty Metal index are likely to react to this beat.

stories.title: US swaps India's expiring 10% tariff for a new 'forced labour' tariff at the same rate
key_points: Old 10% US tariff on Indian goods expired at midnight July 24
Washington immediately replaced it with a new 10% 'forced labour' tariff
India got 10%, not 12.5%, after banning forced-labour-made imports on July 14
17 countries face 10%; China, Japan, UK face a steeper 12.5%
stories.background: In February 2026 the US imposed a temporary 10% across-the-board import surcharge (under a law called Section 122) on most trading partners, capped by law at 150 days. Separately, the US had opened a 'Section 301' probe into whether goods from 60 countries, including India, are made using forced labour, and floated tariffs of up to 12.5% on that basis. India moved on July 14 to amend its Foreign Trade Policy to formally ban imports made with forced labour, hoping to avoid the harsher rate.
stories.what_happened: The 150-day Section 122 surcharge lapsed automatically at 12:01am US time on Friday, July 24, 2026. In its place, the US Trade Representative's office activated a new Section 301 tariff of 10% on Indian goods, citing forced-labour concerns, alongside 16 other countries including Bangladesh, Pakistan, Canada and the UK that also have forced-labour import bans. Countries without such bans, like China, Japan and the UK's non-exempt goods, face 12.5% instead. For India the net rate on affected goods stays at 10%, but on a different, more open-ended legal footing, stacking on top of existing Most-Favoured-Nation tariffs for sectors like textiles, gems, chemicals and engineering goods.
stories.why_it_matters: India avoided a rate hike to 12.5%, but the relief is really about optics, not cost: exporters still pay the same 10% they paid yesterday, just now justified by a labour-standards probe rather than a temporary emergency measure that was always going to expire. That makes the tariff more durable and harder to negotiate away since it isn't tied to a 150-day clock.
stories.ripple_effects: Textile, apparel, gems-and-jewellery and engineering-goods exporters — sectors that dominate India's roughly $87 billion in annual goods exports to the US — face continued margin pressure since the duty stacks on top of normal tariffs; some industry groups warn combined rates on products like polyester fibre could reach 30-40%. Exporters are pushing government relief such as higher interest subsidies on export credit, and New Delhi wants the dispute folded into the ongoing India-US bilateral trade talks rather than resolved unilaterally by the USTR.
stories.why_now: The Section 122 surcharge's statutory 150-day limit expired exactly today, forcing the US to either let tariffs lapse entirely or activate the replacement Section 301 mechanism it had been preparing since a June 3 proposal.
stories.watch_next: Whether India's ongoing bilateral trade negotiations with Washington produce a broader deal that removes or caps the Section 301 duty, and how exporters' Q2 order books react over the next few weeks.

key_terms.definition: A temporary US tariff a president can impose for balance-of-trade reasons, legally capped at 150 days before it must lapse.
A US tariff imposed after a formal investigation into another country's trade practices — unlike Section 122, it has no automatic expiry date.
The 'Most-Favoured-Nation' rate — the normal, baseline import duty a country charges under WTO rules, before any extra surcharges are added.
A law barring the import of goods made using coerced or unfree labour; India adopted one on July 14, 2026 to qualify for the lower US tariff tier.

stories.the_lesson: When a government tariff is set to expire on a legal technicality, don't assume the underlying cost goes away — it can simply be re-issued under a different legal justification, so always check whether relief is structural or just a change in paperwork.
stories.market_link: A durable 10% US tariff keeps pressure on India's export-heavy sectors (textiles, gems, engineering goods) and is a factor markets will weigh alongside the rupee and FII flows into export-facing stocks.

stories.title: Dr Reddy's profit crashes 69% in a quarter, and the stock falls to a 52-week low
key_points: Net profit fell 69% year-on-year to ₹4,435 crore, from ₹14,178 crore
Shares fell nearly 9%, hitting a fresh 52-week low
A ₹240-crore charge on semaglutide (weight-loss/diabetes drug) inventory was a big driver
Lost US lenalidomide sales and rising freight/solvent costs also hurt margins
stories.background: Dr Reddy's is one of India's largest pharmaceutical companies, known for making generic (off-patent, cheaper copy) versions of branded drugs for the US and other markets. Two of its recent growth drivers were semaglutide-based drugs (used for diabetes and weight loss, the active ingredient in drugs like Ozempic) and lenalidomide, a cancer drug whose US exclusivity period for generics has now ended, opening the field to more competitors and crushing the price Dr Reddy's can charge.
stories.what_happened: Dr Reddy's reported its June-quarter results: consolidated net profit dropped 69.2% to ₹4,435 crore from ₹14,178 crore a year earlier, with revenue down more than 5%. The company took a ₹240-crore charge to write down semaglutide-related inventory, while the end of favorable lenalidomide sales and higher freight and solvent costs (raw material and shipping cost pressures, worsened by the West Asia conflict) further squeezed margins. Shares fell nearly 9% on the BSE to a 52-week low.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a sharp reminder that even India's biggest pharma exporters are exposed to US drug-pricing and patent-expiry cycles they don't control — a single ingredient going off-patent or a demand miscalculation can wipe out a large chunk of profit in one quarter.
stories.ripple_effects: Investors are likely to mark down growth expectations for Dr Reddy's near-term earnings and watch its semaglutide strategy closely, since a written-down inventory implies the company overestimated demand. The result also adds to a rough week for Indian markets already reeling from oil-driven selling tied to the Iran war, deepening the market's soured mood on earnings season overall.
stories.why_now: This is Dr Reddy's scheduled quarterly (Q1 FY27) results release, landing in the middle of an already-volatile week for Indian markets driven by external shocks (oil prices, FII selling).
stories.watch_next: Whether Dr Reddy's writes down more semaglutide inventory in coming quarters, and how its US generics pipeline performs as more lenalidomide competitors enter the market.

key_terms.definition: A copy of a brand-name drug, sold once the original's patent protection expires, usually at a much lower price.
The point at which a drugmaker's legal monopoly on selling a drug ends, letting competitors sell cheaper copies and crushing the original maker's pricing power.

stories.the_lesson: A single quarter's profit can swing wildly for a company whose revenue depends on a handful of drugs going on or off patent — that's a structural risk of the generics business model, not a one-off mistake.
stories.market_link: Dr Reddy's Laboratories (NSE: DRREDDY) shares hit a 52-week low; a bellwether read on how the broader pharma/pharma-export basket is faring this earnings season.

stories.title: India's Commonwealth Games campaign hit by doping scandal before it even starts — two athletes withdrawn
key_points: Judoka Arun Kumar tests positive for an anabolic steroid, pulled from Glasgow squad
Weightlifter Dilbagh Singh also withdrawn in the same doping sweep
NADA's out-of-competition test caught Kumar; he gets a provisional suspension
Rules mean India can't even name a replacement for his weight category
stories.background: India had been building toward the Commonwealth Games 2026 in Glasgow (starting July 31) with real medal hopes across boxing, judo, weightlifting and para-sports — several Indian athletes, including Lovlina Borgohain, already have upcoming medal shots lined up. Judoka Arun Kumar, 21, competing in the men's 73kg category, had a strong recent run: gold at the Taipei Asian Open in 2025 and a start at the Qingdao Grand Prix last month.
stories.what_happened: India's National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) said Arun Kumar failed an out-of-competition test, returning an adverse finding for an anabolic steroid. He's been handed a provisional suspension and ruled ineligible for Glasgow. Weightlifter Dilbagh Singh has also been withdrawn from the Games in the same doping-related sweep. The Indian judo team was due to fly out on July 27.
stories.why_it_matters: Beyond the immediate loss of two athletes with real medal potential, a doping case ahead of a major Games embarrasses the whole contingent and invites extra scrutiny — from testers and media alike — on every other Indian athlete competing in Glasgow.
stories.ripple_effects: Competition rules mean Kumar's 73kg judo slot goes empty rather than being handed to a replacement, since the withdrawal came too close to the Games. Team officials will likely face questions about India's anti-doping culture and testing protocols in the run-up to future events, and NADA's case against Kumar will proceed toward a full hearing that could mean a multi-year ban.
stories.why_now: The positive test surfaced from a routine out-of-competition check in the final week before the Indian judo team's scheduled departure for Glasgow.
stories.watch_next: The outcome of NADA's full disciplinary hearing against Arun Kumar, and whether any further athletes are flagged before the Games open on July 31.

key_terms.definition: A temporary ban imposed the moment an athlete fails a drug test, while the full case is investigated — it can later become a multi-year ban or be lifted if the athlete is cleared.
A drug test conducted without warning, away from any event, specifically to catch use during training rather than around a competition.

stories.the_lesson: Anti-doping systems are designed to catch cheating during training, not just on competition day — which is exactly why an athlete can be in career-best form and still get caught, and why a scandal can surface with no warning right before a major event.

stories.title: Assam's flood death toll climbs to 50 as 700,000 people are displaced and Guwahati's roads go under
key_points: Death toll now at least 50, up from 36 a day earlier
700,000 people displaced; nearly 300,000 in relief camps
Almost 900 villages submerged by the overflowing Brahmaputra river
State capital Guwahati (2 million people) had roads flood Thursday evening, stranding commuters
stories.background: Assam sits on the floodplain of the Brahmaputra, one of Asia's largest rivers, which starts in Tibet and flows nearly 900 km through the state. Heavy monsoon rain every year swells the river past its banks, and this year's monsoon has been especially severe — deaths and displacement have been climbing steadily through the week as more districts get hit.
stories.what_happened: Assam's flood death toll has risen to at least 50, up from 36 the day before, with 700,000 people now displaced after days of heavy monsoon rain overflowed the Brahmaputra. Nearly 900 villages have been submerged and more than 7,000 homes lost power. Almost 300,000 people are now in government relief camps. Flooding on Thursday evening disrupted Guwahati, Assam's capital and home to about 2 million people, leaving commuters stranded on submerged roads for hours. Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said authorities are running relief operations including helicopter airdrops of food and supplies.
stories.why_it_matters: This has gone from a serious regional flood to one of the deadliest monsoon disasters India has seen this year, and it's now reaching the state capital itself rather than staying confined to rural districts — meaning the economic and logistical disruption is spreading beyond the immediate humanitarian toll.
stories.ripple_effects: Displaced families lose homes, crops and livestock, often for months; relief spending strains the state budget; and disrupted roads and rail lines through Assam matter nationally too, since the state is a gateway to India's northeast. Insurers and disaster-relief agencies will be watching the death toll and damage estimates as the situation develops.
stories.why_now: The toll roughly kept pace with the river through the week; today's jump to 50 dead and 700,000 displaced — from 36 dead and 650,000 affected just a day earlier — plus flooding reaching the capital for the first time, marks the point where this stopped being a contained district-level problem.
stories.watch_next: Whether the Brahmaputra crests and recedes over the next few days, or whether more rain pushes the death toll and displacement figures higher still.

key_terms.definition: One of Asia's largest rivers, flowing from Tibet through Assam — its annual monsoon swell is the main cause of Assam's recurring floods.

stories.the_lesson: Flood disasters often escalate gradually and get under-covered day to day — but the cumulative toll (villages, displacement, deaths) can end up far larger than any single day's headline suggests, which is why tracking the trend line matters more than any one number.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported the Assam floods had killed 36 people for the week and affected 650,000 across 11 districts, with the toll climbing daily.
thread.changed: The death toll has risen to at least 50 and displacement to 700,000, and the flooding has now reached the state capital Guwahati itself, disrupting roads and stranding commuters for the first time.

stories.title: India's ₹5,000 crore highway-investment trust IPO closes today — its biggest InvIT listing bid yet
key_points: Cube Highways Trust's ₹5,000 crore public offer closes today, priced at ₹151-152 a unit
It's an offer-for-sale — existing owners cashing out, not new money for building roads
Institutional investors get 75% of the units; ordinary retail investors get none
Units list on the NSE and BSE on July 29
stories.background: An InvIT (Infrastructure Investment Trust) is a vehicle that owns income-generating infrastructure — in this case, operating toll roads — and passes most of the toll income straight through to unit-holders as regular payouts, similar to how a REIT works for buildings. Cube Highways, backed by global infrastructure investor I Squared Capital, owns a portfolio of operating toll highways across India.
stories.what_happened: Cube Highways Trust's InvIT public offer, which opened July 22, closes today at a price band of ₹151-152 per unit, targeting roughly ₹5,000 crore. The entire issue is an offer-for-sale of about 32.9 crore units by existing unit-holders — the trust itself raises no fresh money from this sale. Qualified institutional buyers get 75% of the allocation and high-net-worth investors get the rest; ordinary retail investors have zero allocated quota. Units are set to begin trading on the NSE and BSE on July 29.
stories.why_it_matters: This is a real-world example of 'capital recycling': instead of waiting on government budgets, existing investors sell their stake in already-built, already-earning toll roads to public-market investors, freeing up cash to go build the next batch of highways. A strong close signals investor appetite for India's broader pipeline of infrastructure trusts.
stories.ripple_effects: How this IPO gets subscribed and how the units trade on debut will be watched as a bellwether for other InvITs and REITs planning to list, and for how cheaply India's road-building companies can raise future capital. Because retail investors are shut out this time, most of any listing-day gains will flow to institutions rather than everyday investors.
stories.why_now: The offer window (July 22-24) coincides with a wider wave of mid-2026 IPO activity as companies rush to list before the earnings-season lull.
stories.watch_next: The final subscription numbers once the books close today, and how the units trade when they debut on July 29.

key_terms.definition: A publicly listed fund that owns completed infrastructure assets — like toll roads — and pays out most of the income they earn to investors.
An IPO structure where existing owners sell their existing stake to the public, as opposed to the company issuing new shares to raise fresh money.

stories.the_lesson: Infrastructure 'recycling' — selling a completed toll road to public investors — lets a country build more roads with the same pool of money, by turning a slow-return asset into cash the original builder can redeploy immediately.
stories.market_link: Read-through for India's broader InvIT/REIT sector (e.g., IRB InvIT, PowerGrid InvIT) — strong demand here would support more infrastructure-trust listings.

stories.title: Government moves to give 'Vande Mataram' the same legal shield as the National Anthem
key_points: A new Bill would extend the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 to cover the national song
Intentionally insulting or disrupting it could carry up to 3 years in prison — matching the anthem's penalty
Union minister Nityanand Rai tabled it in the Rajya Sabha this Friday afternoon
Congress calls it the government's 'jail first' instinct; BJP frames it as protecting national symbols
stories.background: 'Vande Mataram' — written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay in his 1882 novel Anandmath — was adopted as India's national song (distinct from the national anthem, 'Jana Gana Mana') in 1950. It has a politically loaded history: some Muslim organisations have historically objected to lyrics that personify the nation as a Hindu goddess, while the BJP has long pushed to elevate its status. Parliament marked the song's 150th anniversary with a special Rajya Sabha discussion in December 2025.
stories.what_happened: The Minister of State for Home Affairs, Nityanand Rai, introduced a Bill in the Rajya Sabha on Friday, July 24, to amend the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 so that 'Vande Mataram' gets the same legal protection as the national anthem. Under the proposed amendment, intentionally insulting, obstructing, or disrupting the singing of the song would become a punishable offence carrying up to three years in prison — mirroring the existing penalty for insulting the anthem.
stories.why_it_matters: The Bill would, for the first time, make disrespecting the national song a specific criminal offence rather than just a matter of social convention — raising real questions about where legitimate protest or dissent ends and a punishable 'insult' begins. It also lands amid a broader pattern of the government using national-symbol legislation as a political flashpoint.
stories.ripple_effects: If passed, schools, public institutions and event organisers would need to navigate a new legal risk around how the song is used or skipped. Opposition parties, led by Congress, are expected to contest it, so expect a heated debate — and possibly amendments — as it moves toward the Lok Sabha.
stories.why_now: The push follows the song's 150th-anniversary commemorations in Parliament last December, and comes during the ongoing Monsoon Session where the government has been introducing a cluster of new legislation.
stories.watch_next: Whether the Bill clears the Rajya Sabha and then the Lok Sabha, and how 'intentional insult' ends up being defined in the final law.

key_terms.definition: India has both: 'Jana Gana Mana' is the official national anthem, while 'Vande Mataram' holds the separate, symbolic status of national song.

stories.the_lesson: Laws that criminalise disrespect toward national symbols are rarely just about the symbol — they're usually also a signal of who gets to define patriotism, and a preview of the political fight that follows.

stories.title: Kia launches the Syros EV in India — the first sub-4-metre electric SUV to cross 500km of range
key_points: Base 42kWh Kia Syros EV starts at ₹13.49 lakh ex-showroom — 443km range, 133bhp
Top variant claims 526km range — the first sub-4m EV SUV in India to break the 500km mark
Kia also offers a 'Battery-as-a-Service' plan from ₹7.99 lakh, paying ₹3.8/km for battery use instead of owning it outright
Comes with a 15-year unlimited-km battery warranty and a guaranteed 80% resale buyback after 3 years; deliveries start July 30
stories.background: India taxes cars under 4 metres long at a lower rate than longer ones, so most affordable Indian SUVs — including this one — are deliberately built just under that length to stay cheap. Range anxiety, the fear of running out of charge with nowhere to top up, has been the single biggest reason Indian buyers hesitate on EVs, since most budget electric SUVs here have topped out well below 450km.
stories.what_happened: Kia launched the Syros EV in India, priced from ₹13.49 lakh for the base version. A higher trim claims a 526km range, crossing the 500km mark for the first time in this compact-SUV segment. Kia paired the launch with a 'Battery-as-a-Service' financing option, a long battery warranty, and a guaranteed resale value. Deliveries begin July 30.
stories.why_it_matters: This pushes the entire budget EV segment forward on the one number Indian buyers care about most — range comparable to a full tank of petrol. The Battery-as-a-Service option also experiments with removing the single biggest cost in an EV, the battery, from the upfront purchase price.
stories.ripple_effects: Rivals in the same price band — Tata Motors, Mahindra, Hyundai — face pressure to match or beat this range and warranty package; if buyers respond well to Battery-as-a-Service, other automakers may copy the financing model rather than just the range figure.
stories.why_now: The launch happened yesterday, with deliveries beginning within the week.
stories.watch_next: How rival automakers respond on range and financing terms, and how many buyers actually choose the Battery-as-a-Service plan over an outright purchase.

key_terms.definition: A pricing model where a buyer pays less upfront for the car because they don't own the battery outright — instead paying a per-kilometre fee for its use, similar to a subscription.
India's most popular car size class, kept under 4 metres in length specifically to qualify for a lower tax rate.

stories.the_lesson: In price-sensitive markets, the biggest barrier to adopting a new technology often isn't its performance — it's how it's financed. Separating an expensive component's cost from the purchase price is a classic way to make new technology affordable faster than waiting for it to simply get cheaper.
stories.market_link: Kia's Indian unit competes directly with listed Indian automakers Tata Motors, Mahindra & Mahindra, and Hyundai in the compact electric SUV segment.

stories.title: West Bengal votes today to fill three Rajya Sabha seats vacated by TMC rebels — BJP is expected to sweep them all
key_points: Voting and counting happen today for 3 Rajya Sabha seats from West Bengal
Seats fell vacant after three sitting TMC MPs — Sukhendu Sekhar Roy, Sushmita Dev, and Prakash Chik Baraik — resigned in June
All three quit after publicly questioning TMC's leadership following the party's defeat in West Bengal's assembly election
BJP holds 207 of 293 West Bengal assembly seats, making it near-certain to win all three — since state MLAs, not the public, vote for these seats
stories.background: India's Parliament has two houses: the Lok Sabha, elected directly by voters, and the Rajya Sabha, whose members are instead elected indirectly by sitting state assembly MLAs — so a party's strength in a state assembly translates into seats in Delhi's upper house too, just with a delay. West Bengal recently held state assembly elections, which BJP won decisively; these three Rajya Sabha seats are the first concrete national payoff of that state win, after the sitting TMC MPs holding them resigned rather than stay loyal to a defeated state leadership.
stories.what_happened: Bypolls for the three vacated West Bengal Rajya Sabha seats are being voted on and counted today, July 24. With BJP holding 207 of the state assembly's 293 seats, the party is widely expected to win all three, since West Bengal's MLAs — not the general public — cast the votes.
stories.why_it_matters: A clean sweep moves BJP and its allies closer to a two-thirds majority in the Rajya Sabha — the specific threshold India's constitution requires to pass a constitutional amendment. It converts a state assembly victory into more durable power in Delhi's national law-making, not just West Bengal's state government.
stories.ripple_effects: Strengthens BJP's hand on any future constitutional amendment it wants to push through Parliament; is a further blow to TMC's already-diminished influence at the national level; other opposition parties will be watching how state-level losses keep compounding into Rajya Sabha losses over time.
stories.why_now: The Election Commission scheduled voting and counting for these three seats specifically for today.
stories.watch_next: Today's evening counting result, and whether it's confirmed that BJP/NDA has crossed the two-thirds Rajya Sabha threshold nationally once these three seats are added.

key_terms.definition: The upper house of India's Parliament, whose members are elected indirectly by state assembly legislators (MLAs) rather than by direct public vote.
The higher voting threshold — beyond a simple majority — that India's constitution requires in Parliament to pass a constitutional amendment.

stories.the_lesson: Winning a state election doesn't just hand a party the state government — because Rajya Sabha seats are elected by state MLAs, a state win also reshapes national institutions in Delhi. Power flows upward through the system in ways that take months to show up.

stories.title: Parliament moves to permanently expand the Supreme Court from 33 to 37 judges, replacing a Modi government ordinance
key_points: Lok Sabha takes up the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026 for final consideration and passing today
It raises the Supreme Court's sanctioned strength from 33 to 37 judges (excluding the Chief Justice of India)
It replaces an ordinance President Droupadi Murmu signed on May 16, after the Cabinet approved the expansion on May 5
It needs only a simple majority — Article 124 of the Constitution lets Parliament set judge numbers by ordinary law, not a constitutional amendment
It comes as Opposition members keep up protests over the NEET-UG paper-leak row and a Ram Mandir donation embezzlement case
stories.background: India's Supreme Court has a fixed, government-set number of judges, and a growing backlog of pending cases has long fuelled calls to add more. When Parliament isn't in session, the government can issue an ordinance — a temporary law with immediate effect — but it must get Parliament's approval within months or it automatically lapses. That's what forced this Bill onto the agenda now, during the Monsoon Session.
stories.what_happened: Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal moved the Bill in the Lok Sabha for consideration and passing, seeking to convert May's temporary ordinance into permanent law and lock in the top court's new strength of 37 judges.
stories.why_it_matters: More judges could mean the Supreme Court clears cases faster, cutting years-long delays for litigants. It's also a rare piece of business Parliament is actually moving forward on, even as the Monsoon Session remains gridlocked over unrelated political rows.
stories.ripple_effects: Once the law is confirmed, the collegium (the panel of senior judges that recommends appointments) will need to identify and vet candidates for the four new seats, shaping the Court's composition for years. It follows closely on the heels of the anti-paper-leak Bill also headed to Parliament this session.
stories.why_now: Ordinances lapse if Parliament doesn't ratify them within about six months of being issued, so this Bill has to move during the current session to keep the expanded court legally valid.
stories.watch_next: Passage in the Rajya Sabha (the upper house) next, followed by how quickly the collegium recommends names for the four new judgeships.

key_terms.definition: A law the President can issue when Parliament isn't sitting, which takes effect immediately but must be approved by Parliament within a set time or it lapses.
The panel of senior Supreme Court judges that recommends who should be appointed as judges in India.

stories.the_lesson: Governments can act quickly between parliamentary sessions using ordinances, but those are only a stopgap — they must be ratified by Parliament within months or the temporary law disappears, which is why urgent-sounding ordinances often reappear later as routine-looking bills.

stories.title: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka get a straight run to the Asian Games cricket knockouts
key_points: Four top-ranked sides skip the group stage and go directly to the men's quarterfinals
10-team tournament starts September 24 in Nagoya, Japan
Afghanistan, Japan and Nepal in one preliminary group; Hong Kong, Malaysia and Oman in the other
Women's event runs September 17-22 with 8 teams starting straight at the quarterfinal stage
stories.background: Cricket returned to the Asian Games program in 2023 after a long absence, giving the sport an Olympic-style multi-sport stage in Asia. Not every cricket-playing Asian nation has equal playing strength, so organizers seed the strongest teams directly into the knockout rounds while weaker sides play a preliminary group stage to earn the remaining spots.
stories.what_happened: The International Cricket Council and Asian Games organizers confirmed that India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, as the region's top-ranked sides, will go straight into the men's cricket quarterfinals at the 2026 Asian Games, skipping the preliminary rounds entirely. The 10-team men's competition begins September 24 in Nagoya, Japan, with Afghanistan, Japan and Nepal in one preliminary group and Hong Kong, Malaysia and Oman in the other; the top two from each group join the four seeded teams in the quarterfinals. The women's tournament, held September 17-22 with eight teams, also starts directly at the quarterfinal stage, pairing defending champions India against hosts Japan, Bangladesh against China, Sri Lanka against Malaysia, and Pakistan against Thailand.
stories.why_it_matters: Cricket's growing presence at multi-sport events like the Asian Games, and its Olympic return at Los Angeles 2028, raises the sport's profile beyond its traditional bilateral series and world tournaments, giving smaller cricket nations a rare chance to test themselves against the region's best on a big stage.
stories.ripple_effects: For associate nations like Nepal, Hong Kong and Afghanistan, a good run through the preliminary group could be a genuine confidence and funding boost. For India and Pakistan, a possible knockout-stage meeting adds another high-profile cricket rivalry fixture to an already packed international calendar.
stories.why_now: Organizers finalized the tournament draw and format today as preparations ramp up ahead of the Games opening later this year.
stories.watch_next: The full fixture list and whether India and Pakistan are drawn into the same half of the men's knockout bracket.
stories.the_lesson: Seeding the strongest teams straight into a tournament's knockout stage is a common way organizers balance fairness with giving weaker teams a genuine, winnable path to compete — not every bracket needs everyone to play everyone.

stories.title: West Indies pace bowler Alzarri Joseph turns down Test selection against Pakistan
key_points: Coach Daren Sammy confirms Joseph declined his spot, not just unavailable for 'personal reasons' as first said
Comes right after West Indies named its touring squad with a fresh face in the spin attack
Sammy says the decision is 'way over' his head, leaves it to team directors
The exact personal reasons behind the decision haven't been made public
stories.background: Cricket West Indies named its Test squad for the upcoming series against Pakistan just a day earlier, which included a new spin-bowling option as the team rebuilds its attack. West Indies contracts allow players some ability to decline selection, unlike at many other cricket boards, though it's unusual and puts selectors in an awkward spot.
stories.what_happened: A day after West Indies announced its Test squad to face Pakistan, head coach Daren Sammy confirmed that fast bowler Alzarri Joseph had actually declined his selection, contradicting Cricket West Indies' initial explanation that he was simply unavailable for personal reasons. Sammy said 'Mr Joseph has declined the selection' but did not reveal why, adding that resolving how contracted players can decline selection 'is a decision that is way over my head' and belongs to team directors.
stories.why_it_matters: Losing an established international fast bowler right before a Test series thins out West Indies' pace attack and raises awkward questions about player management and squad discipline, especially as the board scrambles to explain the gap between its first statement and the real story.
stories.ripple_effects: West Indies will likely need to call up a replacement quick bowler on short notice, potentially handing an opportunity to a fringe player. It also pressures Cricket West Indies to clarify its rules around player opt-outs, which could affect how future squads are selected and communicated.
stories.why_now: The story broke because Sammy was asked directly to clarify the discrepancy between the board's 'personal reasons' framing and what actually happened, just as the squad prepares for the Pakistan series.
stories.watch_next: Who replaces Joseph in the final Test squad, and whether Cricket West Indies issues a clearer explanation or policy on player opt-outs.
stories.the_lesson: When an organization's first public explanation doesn't match the full story, the gap itself often becomes bigger news than the original event — vague statements about 'personal reasons' tend to invite more scrutiny, not less.

thread.previously: West Indies named their Test squad to face Pakistan, notable for introducing a new spinner to the attack and naming a first-ever Test venue.
thread.changed: It's now confirmed that quick bowler Alzarri Joseph actually declined his spot in that squad, rather than simply being unavailable as first stated, leaving West Indies to fill the gap before the series.
